extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for U.S. patent practice focused on interference proceedings, new trial/rehearing practice, issuance/form/effect of patents, protests, assignment requirements, and how foreign patents affect term. Aimed at practitioners handling prosecution and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for dissolving an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The grounds on which an interference may be based include the non-patentability of the invention, the absence of priority, and related defects in patentability or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions to dissolve can be grounded on non-patentability, want of novelty, proof of a statutory bar, abandonment by public use, lack of utility (only one invention useful), and similar substantive defects; if the later applicant disclaims the invention the interference will be dissolved (cases cited: Stone v. Greaves; Ex parte Knox; Fuller v. Brush; Hicks v. Keating; Laverty v. Flagg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to dissolve must be based on the application (not outside matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an interference must be based on the application itself alone, and not on the preliminary statement or other outside matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a motion is grounded on 'want of patentability' it must be sent to the primary examiner; motions relying on preliminary statements or outside evidence are improper (Faure v. Bradley; Green v. Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Routing of motions based on non-patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a motion to dissolve an interference is based on want of patentability (or similar grounds) it must be sent to the primary examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner of interferences may suspend and remand the case to the primary examiner, but the examiner of interferences cannot dissolve an interference simply because testimony or arguments were introduced unless it is evident the interference cannot lawfully proceed (Hedges v. Daniels; Green v. Hall). When remanded for want of patentability the interference is dissolved pro hac vice and the applications become ex parte; appeal rights remain as in ex parte cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for filing motion to dissolve
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an interference must be filed within twenty days after the statement is approved, or the delay must be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not filed within 20 days the examiner of interferences will not send the case to the primary examiner unless delay is satisfactorily explained; refusal to send may be appealed to the Commissioner (Green v. Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content required in motion to dissolve
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve must state the reasons, cite the grounds, and show all facts on which the motion is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural sufficiency is required; failure to show facts/grounds will subject the motion to dismissal (Green v. Hall). Adverse parties must be served with notice of the motion and given opportunity to be heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and opportunity to be heard on motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverse parties must be served with a notice of a motion to dissolve an interference and with the reasons therefor, and must have opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process in interference practice requires notice and opportunity to be heard; lack of service may render a motion procedurally defective (Green v. Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular motions to dissolve will be dismissed
rubrics_metrics.description: An irregular motion to dissolve an interference will be dismissed on motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural irregularities (e.g., improper basis, insufficient notice, defective form) can lead to dismissal (Banks v. Snediker and related practice notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to dissolve may be made at any time (subject to rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve may be made at any time, but must meet the procedural and substantive requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although motions can be timely made at varied stages (Banks v. Snediker), substantive grounds based on non-patentability are expected to be raised at the outset; late motions require explanation and may be disfavored.

rubrics_metrics.name: New trials governed by same rules as courts
rubrics_metrics.description: New trials in the Patent Office are granted for the same reasons and with the same restrictions as in other judicial tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal grounds are discovery of new evidence, fraud, or mistake of the tribunal on the real points at issue (Stevens v. Putnam; Wicks v. McAvoy; Eccard v. Drawbaugh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for newly discovered evidence supporting new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly discovered evidence will support a new trial only if it is important, was not previously procurable by due diligence, is not cumulative, proves a new and independent fact, and became known to the party since the former trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All five factors must be satisfied for newly discovered evidence to justify a new trial; failure of due diligence or cumulative nature of the evidence will bar relief (Stevens v. Putnam; Rogers v. Bear).

rubrics_metrics.name: No new trial without due diligence in procuring evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A new trial will not be granted for new evidence unless due diligence had been used to procure it before the former trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If petitioner failed to exercise reasonable diligence or was put on inquiry by prior evidence and failed to apply for a continuance, the petition for new trial will be denied (Rogers v. Bear; Eccard v. Drawbaugh).

rubrics_metrics.name: New trial possible after patent awarded in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A new trial may be granted on the ground of fraud or newly discovered evidence even though a patent has already been awarded to the former successful party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sufficient ground appears (fraud or truly new evidence) the Commissioner may revise the examiner's decision and declare a new interference to re-investigate priority, notwithstanding that a patent was previously issued (Hibbard v. Richmond; Richmond v. Hibbard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on new trial for ignorance/inadvertence/mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: There is conflicting authority whether ignorance, inadvertence, mistake, or surprise (including misstatements by counsel) constitute grounds for a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise notes both that a new trial 'may be granted' for ignorance, inadvertence, mistake, surprise, or misstatements of attorneys, and later that several cases hold such grounds are not sufficient (compare earlier paragraph with Dod v. Cobb; Burdsall v. Curran). Practitioners should rely on controlling precedent in jurisdiction; misstatement by counsel generally is not grounds (Wicks v. McAvoy).

rubrics_metrics.name: New trial for judgment against the weight of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A new trial for a judgment against the evidence will not be allowed unless the judgment is either wholly unsupported by, or is in direct conflict with, the evidence received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard is stringent: only where the former findings are wholly unsupported or clearly in conflict with evidence will a new trial be granted (general practice citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and laches can forfeit right to new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to a new trial may be forfeited by unreasonable delay (laches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay in asserting the right to rehearing/new trial may bar relief (Jones v. Greenleaf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing/new trial waived by appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to a rehearing or new trial is waived by an appeal, even though the appellate court may lack jurisdiction to grant the rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an appeal generally waives the right to seek rehearing/new trial in the lower tribunal; appeal may leave the appellate court without jurisdiction to reopen those matters (Gill v. Scott).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for concurrent tribunals' factual determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent decisions of lower tribunals on questions of fact are not lightly disturbed; they will be set aside only for evident error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On motion for new trial or rehearing, the question is whether former findings are wholly unsupported or in clear conflict; courts/Patent Office give weight to concurrent factual determinations (Hazelup v. Richardson; Gardner v. Dudley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties to interference and role of assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are usually the rival inventors; an assignee may be permitted to prosecute or defend in the inventor's stead when the inventor is unable or refuses to act, or when justice requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission for assignee participation requires motion to the Commissioner and satisfactory evidence showing necessity for such permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue of letters-patent is prima facie judgment of sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of letters-patent is a judgment that all prerequisites have been performed; it is final on mere formal matters and prima facie correct on merits and title, casting the burden of proof on anyone who controverts the presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents constitute prima facie evidence of the facts entitling the patentee to the grant; however, this presumption can be rebutted by proof (Konold v. Klein; Eagleton Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's decision conclusive on formal sufficiency only
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner's decision is final as to the sufficiency of all formal acts and proofs prerequisite to a patent, but is not conclusive on questions on which defenses under the statutes may be made in court (e.g., abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formal regularity is settled by the Patent Office's decision (Mahn v. Harwood), substantive issues relating to the merits and title can be litigated in courts and are not conclusively fixed by the Patent Office determination (Planing Mach. Co. v. Keith; Wilson v. Barnum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral attack limited as to regularity of Patent Office proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The regularity of Patent Office proceedings is, to some extent, conclusive so that a patent cannot be collaterally attacked on such grounds, though irregularities may support repeal in equity or an information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularity is generally presumed in favor of the issued patent; rather than collateral attack, equity/information proceedings are the proper remedy for challenging procedural irregularities (Marsh v. Nichols; cited §§ and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protest against issuance of patent: standing and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A protest against the issue of a patent may be filed by any person and must show that an application has been or will be filed and that the protestant's knowledge of the application was lawfully obtained through voluntary communication by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protests notify the Office of objections and may be used later to rebut presumptions (Ex parte Neale; Er parte Neale). The Commissioner may take any action deemed necessary in response to a protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: To whom patents issue; assignments and timing for assignee entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The grantee is usually the applicant; when an inventor dies a patent issues to executor/administrator; if an applicant assigns the whole interest, the patent may be granted to the assignee upon request, but the assignment must contain an express petition and be recorded at the Patent Office no later than the day the final fee is paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assignment transfers only an undivided interest, the patent may be awarded jointly to applicant and assignee. Timely recordation and express petition are required to secure issuance to an assignee (practice rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and contents of letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent consists of a short title/description correctly indicating nature and purpose, a grant of the exclusive right to make, use, and vend the invention as described in the title and annexed specification, and a copy of the specification and drawings appended and made part of the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No recital of Patent Office proceedings is required; patent must be signed by the Secretary of the Interior and countersigned by the Commissioner; the Secretary's signature is essential to validity and cannot be cured after his term has expired. Patent is not complete until sealed and the Commissioner must affix the seal unless issue would be contrary to law (Hogg v. Emerson; Marsh v. Nichols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date and delivery of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent must bear a date not later than six months from allowance and the mailing of notice and request for the final fee; on payment the patent is prepared, receives its date and number, and is delivered to the patentee or his attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent cannot be antedated; it takes effect from date of issue though it relates back to date of the application for many purposes. The date rules and relation-back have important evidentiary consequences (Gramme Elec. Co. v. Amoux & Hochhausen; Johnsen v. Fassman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of patent privileges governed by statute (and limited by foreign patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a patent is measured by statute, not by the language of the grant; normally seventeen years from grant if not previously patented abroad, but subject to limitation where a prior foreign patent exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. policy limits domestic monopoly so it will not extend beyond the foreign public's right; statutes and case law (acts of 1839, 1861, 1870, 1886, and cases cited) modify how foreign patents affect U.S. term. Under current law the domestic term may be limited to expire at the same time as the foreign patent (but in no event longer than 17 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a foreign patent limits the domestic term
rubrics_metrics.description: To limit the term of the domestic patent by a foreign patent, the inventions covered by the two patents must be identical and the foreign patent must take effect before the issue of the domestic patent (the controlling date is the issue/publication date of the foreign patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The foreign patent limits the domestic whether the foreign protection was open or secret; a domestic patent is not limited by a foreign patent unless the latter claims and describes the same invention; the rule also applies when a U.S. patent covers several inventions separately patented abroad (Gramme Elec. Co.; Holmes Electric Protective Co.; Ex parte Siemens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic patents cannot run beyond statutory maxima
rubrics_metrics.description: An American patent cannot run over seventeen years; limitation by shorter prior foreign patents will cause domestic patent to expire at the earlier time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute (and precedents) ensure the domestic patent term is capped (De Florez v. Raynolds; Weston v. White); specification of term in the grant does not supersede the statutory term.
